pull.body:
> [!NOTE]
> This PR was generated by an AI coding agent (Jetski) on behalf of @mosuem.

_Reopened from #2045 after reordering performance changes behind the `3.2.1` security release (see prior review comments on #2045: [comment 1](https://github.com/dart-lang/http/pull/2045#discussion_r4427012774), [comment 2](https://github.com/dart-lang/http/pull/2045#discussion_r4427024219))._

### Summary

Fixes two `Http2Client` performance regressions against 3.1.0 introduced in 3.2.0. They were found with [`package:http_client_benchmarks`](https://github.com/brianquinlan/http_client_benchmarks) and bisected over every `pkgs/http2` commit since `http2-v3.1.0`:

| Scenario | 3.1.0 | `master` / #2031 | Introduced by | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `download-cancel`: cancel a response after 256 KiB, then make one more request (median, lower is better) | 0.97 ms | 26.3 ms | `be2b51f` #2029 (fixed 4 MiB stream window) | 4.4?4.5 ms |
| `upload-1mib-sequential`: 20 sequential 1 MiB uploads (higher is better) | 27.7 MB/s | 20.7 MB/s | `23f8574` #1999 (1 MiB DATA frames, together with Nagle) | 109?115 MB/s |

All numbers are from a Linux Cloudtop (x64, 48 vCPU), loopback, Dart 3.14.0-dev (JIT), 7 trials + 2 warmup.

1. **A cancelled response held up the connection.** With #2029's fixed 4 MiB stream window, the server has sent up to 4 MiB of a response before the client's `RST_STREAM` reaches it (the benchmark measured at least 1.8 MiB unread). TCP can't skip bytes, so all of that must be received, decrypted and discarded before the response to the next request on the same connection. That costs about 25 ms here, where Dart's TLS manages about 100 MB/s. On an emulated 100 ms / 200 Mbit/s link it added about 55 ms to the next request. On a slow mobile link it would be far worse, because there the drain is bounded by the link's bandwidth.
2. **`Http2Client` never disabled Nagle's algorithm** (see the section below). Since #1999, `Http2Client` honours the peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE`, so an upload to a Go server (1 MiB max frame size) goes out as a single 1 MiB DATA frame. The short tail of that write is then held back by Nagle until the earlier segments are acknowledged. Meanwhile the server delays its acknowledgement (by 40 ms on Linux), because it can't do anything with the frame until the tail arrives. So nearly every upload paid that stall.

### Changes

- **`lib/src/http2_client.dart`**
  - Sets `SocketOption.tcpNoDelay` on every connection, as `dart:io`'s `HttpClient` and `HttpServer` do.
  - Each stream's receive window now starts at 256 KiB (`SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE`) instead of 4 MiB and grows up to 4 MiB as the body is read. The connection window stays at 16 MiB.
- **`lib/src/flowcontrol/window_handler.dart`**
  - `IncomingWindowHandler.stream` takes an optional `maxWindowSize`.
  - When the handler sends a WINDOW_UPDATE (once half the window has been processed), it also adds the current window size to the increment, up to `maxWindowSize`, so the window doubles.
  - Data only counts as processed while the stream's listener isn't paused, so the window only grows while the body is actually being read. Backpressure (#2029) still holds: a paused body holds at most the current window.
- **`lib/src/connection.dart`, `lib/src/streams/stream_handler.dart`**
  - Pass an internal `maxStreamWindowSize` from `ClientConnection` (not exported) to new streams.
  - There is no public API change. `ClientTransportConnection.viaSocket` and `ServerTransportConnection` behave as before.
- **`CHANGELOG.md`**
  - Adds entries under `3.2.2-wip`.
  - Adds an entry for `TCP_NODELAY`.

Not changed: outgoing DATA frames still use the peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE`. I also tried capping them at 16 KiB: with `TCP_NODELAY` it made `upload-large-buffered` 16% slower (122 vs 145 MB/s), so the 1 MiB frames from #1999 are fine once Nagle is off.

### What `TCP_NODELAY` does, and why `Http2Client` should set it

`TCP_NODELAY` is a socket option that turns off **Nagle's algorithm** ([RFC 896](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc896), [RFC 1122 ?4.2.3.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122#section-4.2.3.4)). Nagle is on by default for sockets that `dart:io` creates. While earlier data on a connection is unacknowledged, it makes the kernel hold back any write that doesn't fill a full TCP segment. The held data is sent once everything outstanding is acknowledged, or once enough has piled up to fill a segment. It was designed to stop interactive programs (telnet) from flooding networks with one-byte packets, and on its own it costs at most one round trip.

The problem is how it combines with **delayed acknowledgements** ([RFC 1122 ?4.2.3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122#section-4.2.3.2)). A receiver may hold back its ACK, hoping to piggyback it on response data or to acknowledge two segments at once. Linux holds it for at least 40 ms, and other systems for up to 200 ms. Suppose the sender's last, short segment is waiting for an ACK, and the receiver's ACK is waiting for more data, or for its application to respond, which it can't do without that last segment. Then neither side moves until the delayed-ACK timer fires. This is the classic write-write-read stall.

HTTP/2 hits this all the time, and much more than HTTP/1.1 does:

- Almost every write ends in a short segment: a HEADERS frame, a WINDOW_UPDATE, a SETTINGS or PING ACK, an RST_STREAM, or the tail of a DATA frame.
- Multiplexing puts every request on one connection. So when a new request is written, earlier data on that connection is usually still unacknowledged. With HTTP/1.1 and one request per connection, it usually isn't.

**Should we set it? Yes:**

- **Everyone else does.** `dart:io`'s own `HttpClient` and `HttpServer` call `socket.setOption(SocketOption.tcpNoDelay, true)` on every connection (`sdk/lib/_http/http_impl.dart`). Go's `net` package enables it for all TCP connections by default. curl has enabled it by default since 7.50.2. Without it, moving an app from `IOClient` to `Http2Client` adds latency just because of a missing socket option.
- **It fixes the upload regression and much more.** Measured against #2031 on Linux (one run, compared with `benchmark compare` against two #2031 runs, IOClient control flat):
  - `head-of-line`: 24.4 ms ? 2.6 ms
  - `upload-1mib-sequential`: 20.7 ? 112 MB/s
  - `get-concurrent-16`: 2.9k ? 11.1k req/s
  - `multipart-upload`: 71.9 ? 33.9 ms
  - `download-1mib-sequential`: 62 ? 97 MB/s
  - `many-headers`: 0.97 ? 0.73 ms

  The macOS run of the benchmark doesn't show these stalls (`head-of-line` is 1.7 ms there). Android uses the Linux TCP stack, so it is probably affected; I haven't measured Android.
- **The cost:** with Nagle off, each write goes out at once, so an application that makes many tiny writes sends more, smaller packets. Here that shows up as about 20% fewer requests per second in `get-concurrent-128` (128 tiny requests in flight on one loopback connection; for example 15.3k ? 11.8k req/s). Writes that Nagle used to batch across event-loop turns now go out separately. `FrameWriter` writes every frame to the socket on its own, so batching frames per event-loop turn would be the natural follow-up to win this back. It never adds latency.

### Why a growing stream window, rather than a smaller fixed one

On loopback, the stream window barely matters for throughput once `TCP_NODELAY` is set. It does matter for the cancel cost, and on long links it decides throughput. Each variant below was run once, with `TCP_NODELAY`:

| Stream receive window | `download-cancel` (loopback) | Buffered while paused | 4 MiB download, 100 ms RTT / 200 Mbit/s | 16 MiB download, same link | Cancel + next request, same link |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 64 KiB fixed, no `TCP_NODELAY` (3.1.0's windows)? | 0.97 ms | 36 MiB (no backpressure) | 6,907 ms | 28,911 ms | 103 ms |
| 4 MiB fixed (#2029) | 24.4 ms | 4 MiB | **270 ms** | **827 ms** | 157 ms |
| 1 MiB fixed | 8.8 ms | 1 MiB | 513 ms | 1,983 ms | 103 ms |
| 256 KiB fixed | **1.8 ms** | < 1 MiB | 1,710 ms | 6,812 ms | 103 ms |
| 64 KiB ? 4 MiB | 5.1 ms | < 1 MiB | 794 ms | 1,404 ms | 114 ms |
| **256 KiB ? 4 MiB (this PR)** | 4.8 ms | < 1 MiB | 597 ms | 1,152 ms | 113 ms |
| 1 MiB ? 4 MiB | 8.9 ms | 1 MiB | 411 ms | 967 ms | 103 ms |

Notes on the table:

- The long link was emulated with a userspace proxy adding 50 ms each way and 200 Mbit/s, measured with `Http2Client` on a warm connection, median of 3 downloads and of 5 cancels.
- "Buffered while paused" is what the server had sent while the body was paused. The benchmark can't measure below 1 MiB.
- ? The loopback columns of this row are 3.1.0 itself. Its link columns use this branch with 3.1.0's 64 KiB stream window and Nagle left on.

How to read it:

- A cancelled stream can only have let the server send its current window. With a growing window, that is about twice what the app had read at that point: 640 KiB for a response cancelled after 256 KiB, against 4 MiB before.
- A stream that is read keeps doubling its window about once per round trip and reaches 4 MiB after about 2 MiB, so long downloads still get the large window. Fixed small windows give that up: 256 KiB caps throughput at 256 KiB per round trip.
- The cost against a fixed 4 MiB window is the ramp-up: about 3?4 extra round trips per stream on long links. Starting at 1 MiB would ramp faster but doubles the cancel cost. 256 KiB still fits most API responses and thumbnails within the initial window, and it suits mobile links, where a big window mostly sits in the link's buffers. Changing the start is a one-constant change if reviewers prefer otherwise.

### Benchmarks: full suite, #2031 vs this PR

Same machine, run in ABBA order (#2031, this PR, this PR, #2031). Each round was compared with `dart run bin/benchmark.dart compare`, which uses a Mann-Whitney U test on the 7 trials and reports changes with p < 0.05 and at least 5%. Only `Http2Client` changes; IOClient serves as a control for drift, and it moved by ?5?15% in a few scenarios in either direction, which is normal noise on this VM.

| Scenario (`Http2Client` h2) | #2031 (round 1 / 2) | This PR (round 1 / 2) | Change (round 1 / 2) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `download-cancel` | 21.4 / 22.9 ms | 4.40 / 4.54 ms | **?79% / ?80%** |
| `upload-1mib-sequential` | 21.0 / 20.9 MB/s | 115 / 109 MB/s | **+448% / +423%** |
| `head-of-line` | 22.7 / 22.8 ms | 2.30 / 2.49 ms | **?90% / ?89%** |
| `get-concurrent-16` | 3.1k / 2.9k req/s | 10.6k / 11.6k req/s | **+243% / +304%** |
| `get-delayed-concurrent-100` | 2.5k / 3.0k req/s | 4.6k / 4.5k req/s | **+81% / +54%** |
| `multipart-upload` | 72.0 / 71.8 ms | 32.3 / 31.5 ms | **?55% / ?56%** |
| `download-1mib-sequential` | 61.8 / 63.0 MB/s | 93.9 / 99.0 MB/s | **+52% / +57%** |
| `download-small-writes` | 82.1 / 74.2 MB/s | 106 / 104 MB/s | **+30% / +40%** |
| `upload-streamed-small-chunks` | 103 / 108 MB/s | 131 / 132 MB/s | **+27% / +22%** |
| `many-headers` | 956 / 926 ?s | 713 / 711 ?s | **?25% / ?23%** |
| `download-slow-consumer` (buffered while paused) | 4.0 / 4.0 MiB | < 1 MiB / < 1 MiB | |
| `get-concurrent-128` | 16.3k / 14.4k req/s | 12.6k / 12.1k req/s | **?23% / ?16%** (the `TCP_NODELAY` cost, see above) |
| `upload-large-streamed` | 152 / 156 MB/s | 143 / 146 MB/s | **?6% / ?6%** |

No significant change in both rounds for: `get-sequential`, `get-multi-origin-64`, `download-large`, `download-concurrent`, `server-sent-events`, `upload-large-buffered`, `upload-concurrent`, `cold-client`, `json-burst` and `gzip-download` (+25% in both rounds, but not significant).

### Test Verification (Fails Before ? Passes After)

- `a-response-cancelled-early-had-a-small-window` (new, `test/http2_client_test.dart`): a frame-level server sends as fast as the client's credit allows while the app cancels the body after 256 KiB. The server must have sent ? 1 MiB before the `RST_STREAM` arrives (640 KiB here; 4 MiB before).
- `a-stream-window-doubles-as-the-body-is-read` (new): checks the WINDOW_UPDATE sequence 384 KiB, 768 KiB, 1.5 MiB and 3 MiB (half the window acknowledged plus the window again), then 2 MiB updates at the 4 MiB cap.
- `a-paused-response-body-stops-granting-flow-control-credit` (from #2029, updated): a paused body still grants no credit. The window is now 256 KiB, and resuming grants it back doubled. The test's frame-level server is factored out into `_FrameLevelServer`.
- `incoming-stream-window-grows-up-to-max-window-size` and `incoming-connection-window-does-not-grow` (new, `test/src/flowcontrol/window_handler_test.dart`).

There is no unit test for `TCP_NODELAY`. Nagle stalls depend on timing and on the OS, so they can't be asserted reliably, and the option isn't observable from outside `Http2Client`. The benchmark numbers above cover it.

**Before fix** (new tests on the previous library code):
```text
00:00 +0 -1: http2-client-test a-paused-response-body-stops-granting-flow-control-credit [E]
  Expected: <262144>
    Actual: <4194304>
00:00 +0 -2: http2-client-test a-stream-window-doubles-as-the-body-is-read [E]
  Expected: [393216, 786432, 1572864, 3145728]
    Actual: SubListIterable<int>:[2097152, 2097152]
00:00 +0 -3: http2-client-test a-response-cancelled-early-had-a-small-window [E]
  Expected: a value less than or equal to <1048576>
    Actual: <4194304>
```

**After fix:**
```text
00:00 +10: All tests passed!
```
Full `package:http2` suite at this point of the stack: `+273 ~7: All tests passed!`

### Stack

Stacked on #2111 (release 3.2.1). Followed by #2113 and #2099 (prepare to release 3.2.2).

Reopened from #2045 after reordering performance changes behind the 3.2.1 security release (see prior review comments on #2045: comment 1, comment 2).

Summary

Fixes two Http2Client performance regressions against 3.1.0 introduced in 3.2.0. They were found with package:http_client_benchmarks and bisected over every pkgs/http2 commit since http2-v3.1.0:

Scenario 3.1.0 master / #2031 Introduced by This PR
download-cancel: cancel a response after 256 KiB, then make one more request (median, lower is better) 0.97 ms 26.3 ms be2b51f #2029 (fixed 4 MiB stream window) 4.4?4.5 ms
upload-1mib-sequential: 20 sequential 1 MiB uploads (higher is better) 27.7 MB/s 20.7 MB/s 23f8574 #1999 (1 MiB DATA frames, together with Nagle) 109?115 MB/s

All numbers are from a Linux Cloudtop (x64, 48 vCPU), loopback, Dart 3.14.0-dev (JIT), 7 trials + 2 warmup.

  1. A cancelled response held up the connection. With #2029's fixed 4 MiB stream window, the server has sent up to 4 MiB of a response before the client's RST_STREAM reaches it (the benchmark measured at least 1.8 MiB unread). TCP can't skip bytes, so all of that must be received, decrypted and discarded before the response to the next request on the same connection. That costs about 25 ms here, where Dart's TLS manages about 100 MB/s. On an emulated 100 ms / 200 Mbit/s link it added about 55 ms to the next request. On a slow mobile link it would be far worse, because there the drain is bounded by the link's bandwidth.
  2. Http2Client never disabled Nagle's algorithm (see the section below). Since #1999, Http2Client honours the peer's SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE, so an upload to a Go server (1 MiB max frame size) goes out as a single 1 MiB DATA frame. The short tail of that write is then held back by Nagle until the earlier segments are acknowledged. Meanwhile the server delays its acknowledgement (by 40 ms on Linux), because it can't do anything with the frame until the tail arrives. So nearly every upload paid that stall.

Changes

  • lib/src/http2_client.dart
    • Sets SocketOption.tcpNoDelay on every connection, as dart:io's HttpClient and HttpServer do.
    • Each stream's receive window now starts at 256 KiB (SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE) instead of 4 MiB and grows up to 4 MiB as the body is read. The connection window stays at 16 MiB.
  • lib/src/flowcontrol/window_handler.dart
    • IncomingWindowHandler.stream takes an optional maxWindowSize.
    • When the handler sends a WINDOW_UPDATE (once half the window has been processed), it also adds the current window size to the increment, up to maxWindowSize, so the window doubles.
    • Data only counts as processed while the stream's listener isn't paused, so the window only grows while the body is actually being read. Backpressure (#2029) still holds: a paused body holds at most the current window.
  • lib/src/connection.dart, lib/src/streams/stream_handler.dart
    • Pass an internal maxStreamWindowSize from ClientConnection (not exported) to new streams.
    • There is no public API change. ClientTransportConnection.viaSocket and ServerTransportConnection behave as before.
  • CHANGELOG.md
    • Adds entries under 3.2.2-wip.
    • Adds an entry for TCP_NODELAY.

Not changed: outgoing DATA frames still use the peer's SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE. I also tried capping them at 16 KiB: with TCP_NODELAY it made upload-large-buffered 16% slower (122 vs 145 MB/s), so the 1 MiB frames from #1999 are fine once Nagle is off.

What TCP_NODELAY does, and why Http2Client should set it

TCP_NODELAY is a socket option that turns off Nagle's algorithm (RFC 896, RFC 1122 ?4.2.3.4). Nagle is on by default for sockets that dart:io creates. While earlier data on a connection is unacknowledged, it makes the kernel hold back any write that doesn't fill a full TCP segment. The held data is sent once everything outstanding is acknowledged, or once enough has piled up to fill a segment. It was designed to stop interactive programs (telnet) from flooding networks with one-byte packets, and on its own it costs at most one round trip.

The problem is how it combines with delayed acknowledgements (RFC 1122 ?4.2.3.2). A receiver may hold back its ACK, hoping to piggyback it on response data or to acknowledge two segments at once. Linux holds it for at least 40 ms, and other systems for up to 200 ms. Suppose the sender's last, short segment is waiting for an ACK, and the receiver's ACK is waiting for more data, or for its application to respond, which it can't do without that last segment. Then neither side moves until the delayed-ACK timer fires. This is the classic write-write-read stall.

HTTP/2 hits this all the time, and much more than HTTP/1.1 does:

  • Almost every write ends in a short segment: a HEADERS frame, a WINDOW_UPDATE, a SETTINGS or PING ACK, an RST_STREAM, or the tail of a DATA frame.
  • Multiplexing puts every request on one connection. So when a new request is written, earlier data on that connection is usually still unacknowledged. With HTTP/1.1 and one request per connection, it usually isn't.

Should we set it? Yes:

  • Everyone else does. dart:io's own HttpClient and HttpServer call socket.setOption(SocketOption.tcpNoDelay, true) on every connection (sdk/lib/_http/http_impl.dart). Go's net package enables it for all TCP connections by default. curl has enabled it by default since 7.50.2. Without it, moving an app from IOClient to Http2Client adds latency just because of a missing socket option.

  • It fixes the upload regression and much more. Measured against #2031 on Linux (one run, compared with benchmark compare against two #2031 runs, IOClient control flat):

    • head-of-line: 24.4 ms ? 2.6 ms
    • upload-1mib-sequential: 20.7 ? 112 MB/s
    • get-concurrent-16: 2.9k ? 11.1k req/s
    • multipart-upload: 71.9 ? 33.9 ms
    • download-1mib-sequential: 62 ? 97 MB/s
    • many-headers: 0.97 ? 0.73 ms

    The macOS run of the benchmark doesn't show these stalls (head-of-line is 1.7 ms there). Android uses the Linux TCP stack, so it is probably affected; I haven't measured Android.

  • The cost: with Nagle off, each write goes out at once, so an application that makes many tiny writes sends more, smaller packets. Here that shows up as about 20% fewer requests per second in get-concurrent-128 (128 tiny requests in flight on one loopback connection; for example 15.3k ? 11.8k req/s). Writes that Nagle used to batch across event-loop turns now go out separately. FrameWriter writes every frame to the socket on its own, so batching frames per event-loop turn would be the natural follow-up to win this back. It never adds latency.

On loopback, the stream window barely matters for throughput once TCP_NODELAY is set. It does matter for the cancel cost, and on long links it decides throughput. Each variant below was run once, with TCP_NODELAY:

> [!NOTE]
> This PR was generated by an AI coding agent (Jetski) on behalf of @mosuem.

_Reopened from #2054 after reordering performance changes behind the `3.2.1` security release._

### Summary

Fixes a performance regression against 2.3.1 / 3.1.0 introduced in 3.2.0. The incomplete field-block timeout added in #1958 creates and cancels a `Timer` for **every** inbound HEADERS and PUSH_PROMISE frame, although the whole field block has almost always arrived already. With `package:grpc` (unchanged, Dart AOT, grpc-go as the peer), upgrading http2 from 2.3.1 to #2031 (3.2.0) costs 11?21% of the throughput of small unary RPCs over h2c. Setting `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout: null` recovers all of it, and so does this PR, with the timeout still on:

| Scenario (h2c, RPC/s, median of 35 trials) | 2.3.1 | #2031 (3.2.0) | 3.2.0, `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout: null` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `unary-concurrent-16` (Dart client) | 20.6k | 16.3k (**?21%**) | 20.5k (?0%) | 20.2k (?2%) |
| `many-metadata` (Dart client) | 14.4k | 12.1k (**?16%**) | 14.3k (?1%) | 14.2k (?2%) |
| `server-unary-concurrent-128` (Dart server) | 18.6k | 16.6k (**?11%**) | 18.6k (+0%) | 18.3k (?1%) |

`FrameReader` called `onFieldBlockStart` as soon as it had parsed the 9-byte header of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame. `Connection` armed `Timer(inboundHeaderBlockTimeout)` (10 s by default) there, and cancelled it when the frame with END_HEADERS had been read, usually a few microseconds later in the same chunk of input. That is not free: in the Dart VM, adding a timer that becomes the earliest pending one, and cancelling it again, each send a message to the event handler thread to reschedule the isolate's wakeup (`_Timer._enqueue` / `_Timer.cancel` ? `_notifyEventHandler` in `sdk/lib/_internal/vm/lib/timer_impl.dart`). A busy gRPC client or server usually has no other timer pending, so every RPC paid this once (request headers, on the server) or twice (response headers and trailers, on the client). Over h2c, the Dart worker's CPU time per trial went up by 17?50% in these scenarios, and this PR brings it back to the 2.3.1 level (see below).

### Changes

- **`lib/src/frames/frame_reader.dart`**
  - The reader tracks whether it is inside a field block: from the header of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame up to the end of the frame with END_HEADERS.
  - After it has read all complete frames of a chunk of input, it calls `onFieldBlockIncomplete` (renamed from `onFieldBlockStart`; `FrameReader` is internal) if the input ended inside a field block: in the payload of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame, before a CONTINUATION frame, or inside one. A field block that starts and ends in the same chunk only gets `onFieldBlockEnd`, as before.
- **`lib/src/connection.dart`**
  - Arms the timer from `onFieldBlockIncomplete`. The rest is unchanged: the timer is not re-armed while it runs, so later chunks and CONTINUATION frames don't extend the deadline. It is cancelled when the block is complete (a cheap no-op if it was never armed), and when it fires the connection is terminated with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`.
- **`lib/transport.dart`**
  - The `Settings.inboundHeaderBlockTimeout` docs now say when the timer starts.
- **`CHANGELOG.md`**
  - Adds an entry to the `3.2.2-wip` section.

The protection stays the same. A field block that is not complete within the timeout is terminated with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`. The clock now starts when the reader runs out of input inside the block rather than when it parsed the frame header, which is at most the time it takes to parse the rest of that chunk.

### Benchmarks

`package:grpc` at 7af35c1 (the top of the open grpc-dart stack, no changes) with a `dependency_overrides` for http2. Dart 3.14.0-5.0.dev AOT, grpc-go 1.73 as the peer: Dart client vs Go server for the client scenarios, Go client vs Dart server for `server-*`. Linux Cloudtop (x64, 48 vCPU), loopback. Seven interleaved rounds with the order of the variants rotated each round, `--warmup=1 --trials=5`, so 35 trials per cell. Median (min?max); ?/? = significant (exact two-sided Mann?Whitney U, p < 0.05).

| Scenario | Proto | 2.3.1 | #2031 (3.2.0) | vs 2.3.1 | 3.2.0, timeout `null` | vs 2.3.1 | This PR | vs 2.3.1 | vs #2031 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `unary-concurrent-16` | h2c | 20.6k (14.2k?21.2k) | 16.3k (14.7k?16.7k) | ?21%? | 20.5k (18.6k?21.5k) | ?0% | 20.2k (15.8k?21.1k) | ?2%? | **+24%?** |
| `unary-concurrent-16` | h2 | 18.9k (15.1k?19.3k) | 18.3k (13.6k?19.2k) | ?3%? | 18.6k (8.8k?19.6k) | ?2% | 19.0k (14.8k?20.0k) | +1% | +3%? |
| `many-metadata` | h2c | 14.4k (11.7k?14.8k) | 12.1k (9.6k?12.5k) | ?16%? | 14.3k (10.9k?14.6k) | ?1%? | 14.2k (10.2k?14.8k) | ?2%? | **+17%?** |
| `many-metadata` | h2 | 14.2k (11.5k?15.1k) | 13.1k (8.2k?14.1k) | ?7%? | 13.7k (9.5k?14.6k) | ?3%? | 13.7k (8.6k?15.2k) | ?3%? | +5%? |
| `server-unary-concurrent-128` | h2c | 18.6k (17.5k?19.2k) | 16.6k (13.8k?16.8k) | ?11%? | 18.6k (15.1k?19.0k) | +0% | 18.3k (14.7k?19.1k) | ?1% | **+11%?** |
| `server-unary-concurrent-128` | h2 | 17.9k (13.8k?18.4k) | 17.3k (13.6k?17.9k) | ?3%? | 17.5k (14.3k?18.2k) | ?2%? | 17.6k (14.7k?17.9k) | ?1%? | +2%? |

This PR and `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout: null` are within noise of each other in every row. The remaining 1?3% against 2.3.1 is the same for both, so it comes from other 3.2.0 changes, not from the timer.

- `field-block-callbacks` (new group in `test/src/frames/frame_reader_test.dart`) feeds byte chunks to a `FrameReader` and records the order of its callbacks:
  - `field-blocks-within-one-chunk-are-never-incomplete`: HEADERS + DATA + trailers in one chunk, then HEADERS + CONTINUATION + CONTINUATION + PUSH_PROMISE in one chunk. Only `end` callbacks.
  - `a-frame-split-outside-a-field-block-is-not-incomplete`: a DATA frame split across chunks after a complete HEADERS frame.
  - `headers-payload-split-across-chunks-is-incomplete`: one `incomplete` after the chunk that ends inside the HEADERS payload, then `end`.
  - `push-promise-header-without-payload-is-incomplete`: the same for a PUSH_PROMISE frame header alone.
  - `headers-waiting-for-continuation-is-incomplete`: HEADERS without END_HEADERS, then a chunk ending inside a CONTINUATION frame, then the rest. `incomplete` after each of the first two chunks, then `end`.
- `creates a field-block timer only while a field block is incomplete` (new, `test/server_test.dart`): runs a `ServerTransportConnection` in a zone that records the timers created with the configured timeout. A complete HEADERS frame creates none, and a HEADERS frame whose payload arrives later creates one, which is no longer active once the payload has arrived.
- The existing timeout tests (`terminates an incomplete field block after the timeout`, `starts the field-block timeout before payload completion`) pass unchanged.

**Before fix** (new tests on the previous library code; the reader tests pass the old `onFieldBlockStart` in place of `onFieldBlockIncomplete`):
```text

  Expected: ['end', 'end']
    Actual: ['incomplete', 'end', 'incomplete', 'end']
00:00 +7 -2: field-block-callbacks a-frame-split-outside-a-field-block-is-not-incomplete [E]
  Expected: ['end']
    Actual: ['incomplete', 'end']
00:00 +9 -3: field-block-callbacks headers-waiting-for-continuation-is-incomplete [E]
  Expected: ['incomplete', 'incomplete']
    Actual: ['incomplete']
00:00 +17 -4: server-tests resource limits creates a field-block timer only while a field block is incomplete [E]
  Expected: empty
    Actual: [Instance of '_Timer']
```
(The third failure is expected: the old reader only reported the start of a field block, once.)

**After fix** (`dart test test/src/frames/frame_reader_test.dart test/server_test.dart -n 'field.block'`):

### Summary

Fixes a performance regression against 2.3.1 / 3.1.0 that would otherwise ship in 3.2.0. The incomplete field-block timeout added in #1958 creates and cancels a `Timer` for **every** inbound HEADERS and PUSH_PROMISE frame, although the whole field block has almost always arrived already. With `package:grpc` (unchanged, Dart AOT, grpc-go as the peer), upgrading http2 from 2.3.1 to #2031 (3.2.0) costs 11?21% of the throughput of small unary RPCs over h2c. Setting `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout: null` recovers all of it, and so does this PR, with the timeout still on:

| `unary-concurrent-16` (Dart client) | 20.6k | 16.3k (**?21%**) | 20.5k (?0%) | 20.2k (?2%) |
| `many-metadata` (Dart client) | 14.4k | 12.1k (**?16%**) | 14.3k (?1%) | 14.2k (?2%) |
| `server-unary-concurrent-128` (Dart server) | 18.6k | 16.6k (**?11%**) | 18.6k (+0%) | 18.3k (?1%) |

`FrameReader` called `onFieldBlockStart` as soon as it had parsed the 9-byte header of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame. `Connection` armed `Timer(inboundHeaderBlockTimeout)` (10 s by default) there, and cancelled it when the frame with END_HEADERS had been read, usually a few microseconds later in the same chunk of input. That is not free: in the Dart VM, adding a timer that becomes the earliest pending one, and cancelling it again, each send a message to the event handler thread to reschedule the isolate's wakeup (`_Timer._enqueue` / `_Timer.cancel` ? `_notifyEventHandler` in `sdk/lib/_internal/vm/lib/timer_impl.dart`). A busy gRPC client or server usually has no other timer pending, so every RPC paid this once (request headers, on the server) or twice (response headers and trailers, on the client). Over h2c, the Dart worker's CPU time per trial went up by 17?50% in these scenarios, and this PR brings it back to the 2.3.1 level (see below).

### Changes

- **`lib/src/frames/frame_reader.dart`**
  - The reader tracks whether it is inside a field block: from the header of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame up to the end of the frame with END_HEADERS.
  - After it has read all complete frames of a chunk of input, it calls `onFieldBlockIncomplete` (renamed from `onFieldBlockStart`; `FrameReader` is internal) if the input ended inside a field block: in the payload of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame, before a CONTINUATION frame, or inside one. A field block that starts and ends in the same chunk only gets `onFieldBlockEnd`, as before.
- **`lib/src/connection.dart`**
  - Arms the timer from `onFieldBlockIncomplete`. The rest is unchanged: the timer is not re-armed while it runs, so later chunks and CONTINUATION frames don't extend the deadline. It is cancelled when the block is complete (a cheap no-op if it was never armed), and when it fires the connection is terminated with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`.
- **`lib/transport.dart`**
  - The `Settings.inboundHeaderBlockTimeout` docs now say when the timer starts.
- **`CHANGELOG.md`**
  - Adds an entry to the 3.2.0-wip section.

The protection stays the same. A field block that is not complete within the timeout is terminated with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`. The clock now starts when the reader runs out of input inside the block rather than when it parsed the frame header, which is at most the time it takes to parse the rest of that chunk.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Optional (Draft) PR:** `package:http2` previously chose to terminate connections with `PROTOCOL_ERROR` upon receiving a `PING(ACK)` whose opaque data did not match any locally sent `PING` (`ping-unknown-opaque-data` in `ping_handler_test.dart`). Because [RFC 9113 ?6.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-6.7) specifies that an endpoint *"MUST NOT respond to PING frames containing this flag"* without mandating a connection error, both [`httpwg-cli`](https://github.com/bearcove/loona/tree/main/crates/httpwg) and `h2spec --strict` (`6.7/2`) expect an unsolicited `PING(ACK)` to be ignored while keeping the connection alive. This PR is marked **Draft / Optional** in case maintainers prefer to retain the stricter unknown-`PING(ACK)` rejection.

### Summary

Ignores unsolicited `PING` frames with `FLAG_ACK` set (whose opaque data does not match an outstanding local `ping()`) instead of tearing down the connection with `GOAWAY(PROTOCOL_ERROR)`, while charging unsolicited `PING(ACK)` frames against the connection's `_peerControlFrames` token bucket so floods still terminate with `GOAWAY(ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM)`.

With this optional PR applied:
- **`httpwg-cli` passes 107 / 107 (100%)** of RFC 9113 conformance tests!
- **`h2spec --strict` reaches 143 / 147** (fixing `6.7/2`, up from `142 / 147`).

### Why this is right

- **[RFC 9113 ?6.7 (`PING`)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-6.7):**
  > ACK (0x01): When set, the ACK flag indicates that this PING frame is a PING response. An endpoint MUST set this flag in PING responses. An endpoint MUST NOT respond to PING frames containing this flag.
- **[RFC 9113 ?10.5 (`Denial-of-Service Considerations`)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-10.5):**
  - Solicited `PING(ACK)` frames matching a local `ping()` remain exempt from `_peerControlFrames`, whereas unsolicited `PING(ACK)` frames consume the control/empty-frame token bucket (`ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM` on floods).

- **`lib/src/ping/ping_handler.dart`** ? Return `false` on unmatched `PING(ACK)` instead of throwing `ProtocolException`.
- **`lib/src/connection.dart`** ? Charge `_peerControlFrames` (`_takeControlFrameBudget()`) when `_pingHandler.processPingFrame(frame)` reports an unsolicited `PING(ACK)`.

> [!NOTE]
> This PR was generated by an AI coding agent (Jetski) on behalf of @mosuem.

### Summary

Running [`httpwg-cli`](https://github.com/bearcove/loona/tree/main/crates/httpwg) (`bearcove/loona`'s RFC 9113 conformance suite) against `package:http2` surfaced three remaining RFC 9113 conformance and security issues not covered by `h2spec`:
1. **`Host` vs. `:authority` mismatch (`H2.Host` smuggling, [RFC 9113 ?8.3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.3.1)):** A request carrying both `:authority` and a `host` header identifying a different authority (or duplicate `host` headers, or userinfo `@`) was accepted instead of rejected with `RST_STREAM(PROTOCOL_ERROR)`, creating a routing/origin mismatch if translated to HTTP/1.1 downstream.
2. **Incomplete client `PUSH_PROMISE` buffered on servers ([RFC 9113 ?8.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.4)):** When a client sent a `PUSH_PROMISE` frame without `END_HEADERS`, `Connection._handleFrameImpl` passed it into `FrameDefragmenter` before checking `!isClientConnection`, buffering fragments until `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout` instead of immediately terminating with `GOAWAY(PROTOCOL_ERROR)`.
3. **`HEADERS` on an already-closed stream reported `PROTOCOL_ERROR` instead of `STREAM_CLOSED` ([RFC 9113 ?5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-5.1)):** Re-sending `HEADERS` on a previously opened and closed stream ID (`<= lastRemoteStreamId`) fell through `_registerNewRemoteStreamId`'s generic `PROTOCOL_ERROR` check instead of returning `GOAWAY(STREAM_CLOSED)`.

With this PR, `httpwg-cli` passes **106 / 107** RFC 9113 tests (up from 57 / 107 in `3.1.0` and 102 / 107 on #2108; the single remaining test is unsolicited `PING(ACK)`, which `PingHandler` intentionally treats as `PROTOCOL_ERROR` per `ping_handler_test.dart`).

### Why this is right

- **[RFC 9113 ?8.3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.3.1) & [RFC 3986 ?6.2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986#section-6.2.3):**
  > ":authority" MUST NOT include the deprecated userinfo subcomponent for "http" or "https" schemed URIs.
  > [...]
  > A server SHOULD treat a request as malformed if it contains a Host header field that identifies an entity that differs from the entity in the ":authority" pseudo-header field. The values of fields need to be normalized to compare them (see Section 6.2 of [RFC3986]). An origin server can apply any normalization method, whereas other servers MUST perform scheme-based normalization (see Section 6.2.3 of [RFC3986]) of the two fields.
- **[RFC 9113 ?8.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.4):**
  > A client cannot push. Thus, servers MUST treat the receipt of a PUSH_PROMISE frame as a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.
- **[RFC 9113 ?5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-5.1) vs. [?5.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-5.1.1):**
  - Receiving `HEADERS` on a stream that transitioned to `closed` is a connection error of type `STREAM_CLOSED` (?5.1).
  - Receiving `HEADERS` on a lower unused stream ID that was implicitly skipped when a higher stream ID opened remains a connection error of type `PROTOCOL_ERROR` (?5.1.1).

### Changes

- **`lib/src/streams/http_message_validator.dart`**
  - Reject `host` in trailers, duplicate `host` headers, userinfo (`@`) in `host` or `http(s)` `:authority`, and requests where scheme-normalized `host` disagrees with `:authority`.
- **`lib/src/connection.dart`**
  - Reject `PushPromiseFrame` on server connections before `_defragmenter.tryDefragmentFrame`, and map `ConnectionStreamClosedException` to `GOAWAY(STREAM_CLOSED)`.
- **`lib/src/sync_errors.dart`, `lib/src/streams/stream_handler.dart`**
  - Track a bounded 256-entry `LinkedHashSet` of recently opened remote stream IDs so `HEADERS` on an already-closed stream raises `ConnectionStreamClosedException` (`STREAM_CLOSED`) while skipped lower stream IDs continue to raise `ProtocolException` (`PROTOCOL_ERROR`).

  - Add 4 server tests and `3.2.1-wip` changelog entry.

HEADERS on an already-closed stream reported PROTOCOL_ERROR instead of STREAM_CLOSED (RFC 9113 ?5.1): Re-sending HEADERS on a previously opened and closed stream ID (<= lastRemoteStreamId) fell through _registerNewRemoteStreamId's generic PROTOCOL_ERROR check instead of returning GOAWAY(STREAM_CLOSED).

":authority" MUST NOT include the deprecated userinfo subcomponent for "http" or "https" schemed URIs.
[...]
A server SHOULD treat a request as malformed if it contains a Host header field that identifies an entity that differs from the entity in the ":authority" pseudo-header field. A client cannot push. Thus, servers MUST treat the receipt of a PUSH_PROMISE frame as a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.

### Summary

Hardens `Http2Client` (`package:http2/client.dart`) across four areas:
1. **Outbound request validation & IPv6 `:authority` bracketing:** Validates URL authority, HTTP method token, and request header names/values before dialing (rejecting `:`-prefixed pseudo-header injection, CR/LF/NUL/CTLs, and `te` values other than `trailers`, and stripping fields nominated by `Connection`), and encloses IPv6 literals in square brackets (`[::1]:port`) in `:authority` and pool keys.
2. **Response header state machine:** Requires a valid 3-digit `:status` (`100..599`, excluding `101`), ignores `1xx` informational headers instead of merging them into `StreamedResponse.headers`, ignores trailing `HEADERS` instead of mutating `responseHeaders`, rejects `DATA` arriving before `:status`, and resets the stream on protocol errors.
3. **Unread response-body backpressure:** Pauses the underlying stream subscription as soon as final response headers arrive until `response.stream` is listened to, preventing an unread `StreamedResponse` from auto-granting `WINDOW_UPDATE`s up to 4 MiB and buffering unbounded `DATA` inside `bodyController`.
4. **Full-connection liveness (`ClientConnection.isAlive`):** Distinguishes a dead/finishing connection from one that is merely at its `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` capacity so a single-stream `RST_STREAM` on a full connection does not poison and evict the connection from `ClientPool`.

> [!NOTE]
> This PR was generated by an AI coding agent (Jetski) on behalf of @mosuem.

### Summary

Hardens HPACK decoding, `CONTINUATION` frame defragmentation, and inbound HTTP/2 field and message validation against HTTP/2-to-HTTP/1.1 request smuggling (`H2.CL`, `H2.TE`, `H2.CRLF` ? CVE-2021-33197, CVE-2022-22720, CVE-2023-25690) and RFC 7541 / RFC 9113 conformance gaps:
1. **HPACK decoder (`lib/src/hpack/hpack.dart`):**
   - Reject variable-length integers that overflow 31 bits instead of wrapping negative on 64-bit Dart ints ([RFC 7541 ?5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7541#section-5.1)).
   - Reject dynamic table size updates appearing after header fields in a block ([RFC 7541 ?4.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7541#section-4.2), `h2spec` `hpack/4.2/1`).
   - Empty the dynamic table when an indexed entry exceeds `_maximumSize` ([RFC 7541 ?4.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7541#section-4.4)) and copy compact `Uint8List` slices into dynamic table entries so long-lived entries cannot pin multi-hundred-KiB defragmented header-block buffers.
2. **`CONTINUATION` framing (`lib/src/frames/frame_defragmenter.dart`, `lib/src/streams/stream_handler.dart`):**
   - Treat unsolicited `CONTINUATION` frames on idle/closed streams as connection errors of type `PROTOCOL_ERROR` ([RFC 9113 ?6.10](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-6.10), `h2spec` `5.1/4`, `5.1/13`, `6.10/4?5`).
   - Mask `CONTINUATION` flags to `FLAG_END_HEADERS` (`0x04`) when completing a field block so undefined flags (such as `0x01`, `END_STREAM` on `HEADERS`) cannot forge `END_STREAM` ([RFC 9113 ?4.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-4.1)).
3. **HTTP/2 field & `content-length` validation (`lib/src/streams/http_message_validator.dart`, `lib/src/streams/stream_handler.dart`):**
   - Validate lowercase `tchar` header names ([RFC 9113 ?8.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.2.1), `h2spec` `8.1.2/1`), forbid `NUL`/`CR`/`LF`/CTLs and leading/trailing `SP`/`HTAB` in header values (`H2.CRLF`), reject forbidden connection-specific headers (`connection`, `proxy-connection`, `keep-alive`, `transfer-encoding`, `upgrade`, and `te` unless `'trailers'`, [RFC 9113 ?8.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.2.2), `H2.TE`), validate pseudo-header ordering/uniqueness/types/completeness ([RFC 9113 ??8.3?8.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.3)), require `END_STREAM` on trailer `HEADERS` ([RFC 9113 ?8.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.1), `h2spec` `8.1/1`), and enforce `content-length` against received `DATA` byte sums ([RFC 9113 ?8.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.1.1), `H2.CL`, `h2spec` `8.1.2.6/1?2`).

### Why this is right

Per [RFC 9113 ?8.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.1.1), [?8.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.2.1), [?8.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-8.2.2), and [?10.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-10.3):

> Malformed requests or responses that are detected MUST be treated as a stream error (Section 5.4.2) of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.
> [...]
> A request or response is also malformed if the value of a content-length header field does not equal the sum of the DATA frame payload lengths that form the content, unless the message is defined as having no content.
> [...]
> A field value MUST NOT contain the zero value (ASCII NUL, 0x00), line feed (ASCII LF, 0x0a), or carriage return (ASCII CR, 0x0d) at any position. A field value MUST NOT start or end with an ASCII whitespace character (ASCII SP or HTAB, 0x20 or 0x09).
> [...]

> [!NOTE]
> This PR was generated by an AI coding agent (Jetski) on behalf of @mosuem.

### Summary

Fixes three outbound buffering and fragmentation vulnerabilities:
1. **Internal Data Buffering (CVE-2019-9517):** `StreamMessageQueueOut` checked only `streamWindow.peerWindowSize` before draining all outgoing `DataMessage`s into `ConnectionMessageQueueOut._messages` and marking `stream.outgoingQueue.bufferIndicator` unbuffered. A peer advertising a huge `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (`2^31 - 1`) while withholding connection `WINDOW_UPDATE`s (or not reading from its TCP socket) caused `stream.outgoingMessages.addStream(...)` to never pause, buffering arbitrary response data in memory.
2. **Unread `WINDOW_UPDATE` reply accumulation:** `FrameWriter.writeWindowUpdate` bypassed `_writeReplyFrame`, so a peer sending `DATA` frames on a drained stream without reading from the socket could queue `WINDOW_UPDATE` replies past `FrameWriter.maxQueuedReplyFrames`.
3. **Quadratic `List.sublist` copying on Data Dribble (CVE-2019-9511):** When an application passed a non-`Uint8List` `List<int>` to `sendData` and a peer granted 1-byte `WINDOW_UPDATE` increments, `viewOrSublist` fell back to `List.sublist` on every byte, copying `O(N^2)` elements.

### Why this is right

Per [RFC 9113 ?10.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-10.5):

> Providing tiny increments to flow control in WINDOW_UPDATE frames can cause a sender to generate a large number of DATA frames.
> [...]
> An attacker can provide large amounts of flow-control credit at the HTTP/2 layer but withhold credit at the TCP layer, preventing frames from being sent. An endpoint that constructs and remembers frames for sending without considering TCP limits might be subject to resource exhaustion.

Propagating `ConnectionMessageQueueOut.dataBufferIndicator` to `StreamMessageQueueOut` pauses `stream._outgoingCSubscription` as soon as the connection send window or underlying transport sink blocks, count-limiting unread `WINDOW_UPDATE` replies enforces `maxQueuedReplyFrames`, and normalizing larger non-`Uint8List` `DataMessage` payloads once to `Uint8List` makes every subsequent `viewOrSublist` slice an `O(1)` `Uint8List.view`.

### Changes

- **`lib/src/flowcontrol/connection_queues.dart`, `lib/src/flowcontrol/stream_queues.dart`, `lib/src/streams/stream_handler.dart`**
  - Expose `ConnectionMessageQueueOut.dataBufferIndicator` and hold non-empty `DataMessage`s in `StreamMessageQueueOut` while connection-level sending would buffer, propagating pause/resume signals to `stream.outgoingMessages`.
- **`lib/src/frames/frame_writer.dart`**
  - Route `writeWindowUpdate` through `_writeReplyFrame`.
- **`lib/src/flowcontrol/queue_messages.dart`**
  - Normalize non-`Uint8List` `DataMessage` byte lists (`length > 64`) once into `Uint8List`.
- **`test/server_test.dart`, `test/src/flowcontrol/stream_queues_test.dart`, `test/src/flowcontrol/mocks.mocks.dart`, `CHANGELOG.md`**
  - Add backpressure, unread-`WINDOW_UPDATE`, and linear-dribble tests plus `3.2.1-wip` changelog entry.

commit.message:
fix(http2): Http2Client disables Nagle's algorithm and grows each stream's receive window from 256 KiB

Fixes two Http2Client performance regressions against 3.1.0, found with
package:http_client_benchmarks and bisected to their commits:

- download-cancel (cancel a response after 256 KiB, then make one more
  request on the same client): ~1 ms in 3.1.0, ~26 ms since #2029. With a
  fixed 4 MiB stream window the server has already sent up to 4 MiB of the
  cancelled response, all of which must be read off the shared connection
  before the next response. Each stream's receive window now starts at
  256 KiB and doubles every time half of it has been read, up to 4 MiB: a
  response that is cancelled (or paused) early has only let the server send a
  little, while a long download still reaches the 4 MiB window.
- upload-1mib-sequential: 27.7 MB/s in 3.1.0, 20.7 MB/s since #1999.
  Http2Client never disabled Nagle's algorithm, which holds back the short
  tail of a write until the earlier data is acknowledged, while the server
  delays that acknowledgement (by 40 ms on Linux) waiting for the rest of the
  frame. Since #1999 an upload is sent as one large DATA frame, so this
  stalled nearly every upload. Http2Client now sets TCP_NODELAY, as dart:io's
  HttpClient and HttpServer do; that also removes the same stall from many
  other requests (e.g. head-of-line latency 24 ms -> 2.6 ms on Linux).

The growing window is internal to Http2Client: ClientConnection (not
exported) takes a maxStreamWindowSize that the stream handler passes to each
stream's IncomingWindowHandler.

pull.body:
Fixes #1997.

A connection on `package:http2` moved at most 64 KiB per round trip: the
connection receive window is fixed at the protocol's 65535 bytes, so
`streamWindowSize` alone cannot raise throughput. With a 4 MiB body from a
Go `net/http` server and 100 ms of added round-trip time, `dart:io`'s
HTTP/1.1 client took ~350 ms and this package's client 7.1 s.

The new settings live on `Settings`, so they apply to clients and servers
alike:

- `Settings.connectionWindowSize` (65535..2147483647) grants a larger
  connection window with a WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0 after the initial
  SETTINGS.
- `Settings.maxFrameSize` is sent as `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE`.
- A larger initial `streamWindowSize`, and `maxFrameSize`, apply to this
  end's receive side from the moment they are sent: a peer that has not read
  them yet stays within the defaults, which they still allow. Waiting for the
  ACK capped every early response's first round trip at 64 KiB. A smaller
  `streamWindowSize` still applies on ACK, since a client may send before it
  has read the server's SETTINGS (RFC 9113 section 3.4).
- From twice the default window, received data is acknowledged once per half
  window rather than once per DATA frame (the TODO in
  `IncomingWindowHandler.dataProcessed`); smaller windows are acknowledged
  at once, as before.
- The new settings are validated up front in `_validateSettings`.

Fixed on the way (from review): the peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` is
honored when sending and refused outside 16384..16777215; the ACK of this
end's own `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` no longer resizes send windows; a
WINDOW_UPDATE of 0 is never sent.

Defaults are unchanged; whether a client should default to larger values
can be taken up separately once this has landed. With `streamWindowSize`
6 MiB, `connectionWindowSize` 16 MiB and `maxFrameSize` 1 MiB the transfer
above takes ~340 ms (~140 ms without added delay, against ~155 ms for
HTTP/1.1).

Tests: `test/flow_control_test.dart` drives a raw peer and checks each
behaviour on the wire, using a PING round trip (not a sleep) wherever it
asserts that a frame was not sent; `settings_handler_test.dart` and
`window_handler_test.dart` cover the review fixes. Each test fails with its
part of the change removed. `dart analyze --fatal-infos`, `dart format` and
the full `dart test` pass (254 tests).

- [x] I've reviewed the contributor guide and applied the relevant portions to this PR.

pull.body:
> [!NOTE]
> This PR was generated by an AI coding agent (Jetski) on behalf of @mosuem.

### Summary

`Http2Client` forwarded every `DATA` frame of a response into the `StreamController` behind `StreamedResponse.stream` regardless of whether anyone was reading it. The HTTP/2 stream's subscription was never paused, so the stream kept acknowledging data with `WINDOW_UPDATE` frames (RFC 9113 Section 5.2) and the server kept sending: a consumer that paused the body ? or simply read it slower than the network delivered it ? accumulated the entire response in memory. HTTP/2 flow control exists precisely so that a receiver can stop granting credit when it is not consuming.

Separately, the client used the protocol's default 65535-byte windows, which cap a connection at 64 KiB per round trip no matter how many streams it carries.

### Changes

- **`lib/src/http2_client.dart`**
  - `bodyController` now forwards `onPause`/`onResume` to the HTTP/2 stream's subscription. The stream's incoming queue then stops dispatching (`StreamMessageQueueIn._tryDispatch` only dispatches to a non-paused listener, and it is dispatching that calls `windowHandler.dataProcessed`, i.e. sends `WINDOW_UPDATE`), so once the data the server was already allowed to send has arrived it must wait. Memory held by a paused body is bounded by the stream window; across all of a connection's paused streams by the connection window.
  - `_dial` configures `ClientSettings(streamWindowSize: 4 MiB, connectionWindowSize: 16 MiB)`. The two changes belong together: with backpressure and the 64 KiB *connection* window, one paused body would exhaust the connection's credit and stall every other stream on it (the connection queue stops handing data to a buffering stream and only replenishes connection credit for data it handed over).

Not changed, as candidates for follow-ups: a body that has not been listened to yet is still buffered without bound (pausing the HTTP/2 subscription until the first listener would delay `onDone`, and with it the pool slot's release, for callers that never read the body ? a behavior change worth its own discussion); and whether the window sizes should be `Http2Client` constructor parameters rather than constants.

### Test Verification (Fails Before $\rightarrow$ Passes After)

`a-paused-response-body-stops-granting-flow-control-credit` in `test/http2_client_test.dart`, against a frame-level TLS server (`FrameReader`/`FrameWriter` on the accepted socket), with no sleeps:

1. Asserts the client's SETTINGS advertise a 4 MiB stream window and its stream-0 `WINDOW_UPDATE` raises the connection window to 16 MiB.
2. Sends the response HEADERS, pauses the body subscription, then sends exactly the stream window (4 MiB) of `DATA` followed by a PING. The client answers the PING only after processing every frame before it, so any stream `WINDOW_UPDATE` arriving before the PING ACK was granted while paused.
3. Resumes the body and waits for the full window to be granted back, then sends the final `DATA` with `END_STREAM` and checks the body is complete (4 MiB + 3 bytes).

**Before fix** (test on the previous library code ? fails at step 1):
```text
00:00 +0 -1: http2-client-test a-paused-response-body-stops-granting-flow-control-credit [E]
  Expected: <4194304>
    Actual: <null>
```
With only the window sizes applied (no `onPause`/`onResume` forwarding) it fails at step 2, at the first half-window acknowledgement:
```text
00:00 +0 -1: http2-client-test a-paused-response-body-stops-granting-flow-control-credit [E]
  The client granted 2097152 bytes of credit while the response body was paused.
```

**After fix:**
```text
00:00 +1: All tests passed!
```

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `download-cancel`: cancel a response after 256 KiB, then make one more request (median, lower is better) | 0.97 ms | 26.3 ms | `be2b51f` #2029 (fixed 4 MiB stream window) | 4.4?4.5 ms |

`TCP_NODELAY` is a socket option that turns off **Nagle's algorithm** ([RFC 896](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc896), [RFC 1122 ?4.2.3.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122#section-4.2.3.4)). HTTP/2 hits this all the time, and much more than HTTP/1.1 does:

- Almost every write ends in a short segment: a HEADERS frame, a WINDOW_UPDATE, a SETTINGS or PING ACK, an RST_STREAM, or the tail of a DATA frame.

  - `upload-1mib-sequential`: 20.7 ? 112 MB/s
  - `get-concurrent-16`: 2.9k ? 11.1k req/s

  - `download-1mib-sequential`: 62 ? 97 MB/s

issue.body_html:
Note

This PR was generated by an AI coding agent (Jetski) on behalf of @mosuem.

Summary

Fixes two Http2Client performance regressions against 3.1.0 that would otherwise ship in 3.2.0. They were found with package:http_client_benchmarks and bisected over every pkgs/http2 commit since http2-v3.1.0:

Scenario 3.1.0 master / #2031 Introduced by This PR
download-cancel: cancel a response after 256 KiB, then make one more request (median, lower is better) 0.97 ms 26.3 ms be2b51f #2029 (fixed 4 MiB stream window) 4.4?4.5 ms
upload-1mib-sequential: 20 sequential 1 MiB uploads (higher is better) 27.7 MB/s 20.7 MB/s 23f8574 #1999 (1 MiB DATA frames, together with Nagle) 109?115 MB/s

All numbers are from a Linux Cloudtop (x64, 48 vCPU), loopback, Dart 3.14.0-dev (JIT), 7 trials + 2 warmup.

  1. A cancelled response held up the connection. With #2029's fixed 4 MiB stream window, the server has sent up to 4 MiB of a response before the client's RST_STREAM reaches it (the benchmark measured at least 1.8 MiB unread). TCP can't skip bytes, so all of that must be received, decrypted and discarded before the response to the next request on the same connection. That costs about 25 ms here, where Dart's TLS manages about 100 MB/s. On an emulated 100 ms / 200 Mbit/s link it added about 55 ms to the next request. On a slow mobile link it would be far worse, because there the drain is bounded by the link's bandwidth.
  2. Http2Client never disabled Nagle's algorithm (see the section below). Since #1999, Http2Client honours the peer's SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE, so an upload to a Go server (1 MiB max frame size) goes out as a single 1 MiB DATA frame. The short tail of that write is then held back by Nagle until the earlier segments are acknowledged. Meanwhile the server delays its acknowledgement (by 40 ms on Linux), because it can't do anything with the frame until the tail arrives. So nearly every upload paid that stall.

Changes

  • lib/src/http2_client.dart
    • Sets SocketOption.tcpNoDelay on every connection, as dart:io's HttpClient and HttpServer do.
    • Each stream's receive window now starts at 256 KiB (SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE) instead of 4 MiB and grows up to 4 MiB as the body is read. The connection window stays at 16 MiB.
  • lib/src/flowcontrol/window_handler.dart
    • IncomingWindowHandler.stream takes an optional maxWindowSize.
    • When the handler sends a WINDOW_UPDATE (once half the window has been processed), it also adds the current window size to the increment, up to maxWindowSize, so the window doubles.
    • Data only counts as processed while the stream's listener isn't paused, so the window only grows while the body is actually being read. Backpressure (#2029) still holds: a paused body holds at most the current window.
  • lib/src/connection.dart, lib/src/streams/stream_handler.dart
    • Pass an internal maxStreamWindowSize from ClientConnection (not exported) to new streams.
    • There is no public API change. ClientTransportConnection.viaSocket and ServerTransportConnection behave as before.
  • CHANGELOG.md
    • Updates the Http2Client window entry from #2029 to describe the final 3.2.0 behaviour.
    • Adds an entry for TCP_NODELAY.

Not changed: outgoing DATA frames still use the peer's SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE. I also tried capping them at 16 KiB: with TCP_NODELAY it made upload-large-buffered 16% slower (122 vs 145 MB/s), so the 1 MiB frames from #1999 are fine once Nagle is off.

What TCP_NODELAY does, and why Http2Client should set it

TCP_NODELAY is a socket option that turns off Nagle's algorithm (RFC 896, RFC 1122 ?4.2.3.4). Nagle is on by default for sockets that dart:io creates. While earlier data on a connection is unacknowledged, it makes the kernel hold back any write that doesn't fill a full TCP segment. The held data is sent once everything outstanding is acknowledged, or once enough has piled up to fill a segment. It was designed to stop interactive programs (telnet) from flooding networks with one-byte packets, and on its own it costs at most one round trip.

The problem is how it combines with delayed acknowledgements (RFC 1122 ?4.2.3.2). A receiver may hold back its ACK, hoping to piggyback it on response data or to acknowledge two segments at once. Linux holds it for at least 40 ms, and other systems for up to 200 ms. Suppose the sender's last, short segment is waiting for an ACK, and the receiver's ACK is waiting for more data, or for its application to respond, which it can't do without that last segment. Then neither side moves until the delayed-ACK timer fires. This is the classic write-write-read stall.

HTTP/2 hits this all the time, and much more than HTTP/1.1 does:

  • Almost every write ends in a short segment: a HEADERS frame, a WINDOW_UPDATE, a SETTINGS or PING ACK, an RST_STREAM, or the tail of a DATA frame.
  • Multiplexing puts every request on one connection. So when a new request is written, earlier data on that connection is usually still unacknowledged. With HTTP/1.1 and one request per connection, it usually isn't.

Should we set it? Yes:

  • Everyone else does. dart:io's own HttpClient and HttpServer call socket.setOption(SocketOption.tcpNoDelay, true) on every connection (sdk/lib/_http/http_impl.dart). Go's net package enables it for all TCP connections by default. curl has enabled it by default since 7.50.2. Without it, moving an app from IOClient to Http2Client adds latency just because of a missing socket option.

  • It fixes the upload regression and much more. Measured against #2031 on Linux (one run, compared with benchmark compare against two #2031 runs, IOClient control flat):

    • head-of-line: 24.4 ms ? 2.6 ms
    • upload-1mib-sequential: 20.7 ? 112 MB/s
    • get-concurrent-16: 2.9k ? 11.1k req/s
    • multipart-upload: 71.9 ? 33.9 ms
    • download-1mib-sequential: 62 ? 97 MB/s
    • many-headers: 0.97 ? 0.73 ms

    The macOS run of the benchmark doesn't show these stalls (head-of-line is 1.7 ms there). Android uses the Linux TCP stack, so it is probably affected; I haven't measured Android.

  • The cost: with Nagle off, each write goes out at once, so an application that makes many tiny writes sends more, smaller packets. Here that shows up as about 20% fewer requests per second in get-concurrent-128 (128 tiny requests in flight on one loopback connection; for example 15.3k ? 11.8k req/s). Writes that Nagle used to batch across event-loop turns now go out separately. FrameWriter writes every frame to the socket on its own, so batching frames per event-loop turn would be the natural follow-up to win this back. It never adds latency.

Why a growing stream window, rather than a smaller fixed one

On loopback, the stream window barely matters for throughput once TCP_NODELAY is set. It does matter for the cancel cost, and on long links it decides throughput. Each variant below was run once, with TCP_NODELAY:

1 MiB fixed 8.8 ms 1 MiB 513 ms 1,983 ms 103 ms
256 KiB fixed 1.8 ms < 1 MiB 1,710 ms 6,812 ms 103 ms
64 KiB ? 4 MiB 5.1 ms < 1 MiB 794 ms 1,404 ms 114 ms
256 KiB ? 4 MiB (this PR) 4.8 ms < 1 MiB 597 ms 1,152 ms 113 ms
1 MiB ? 4 MiB 8.9 ms 1 MiB 411 ms 967 ms 103 ms

  • The long link was emulated with a userspace proxy adding 50 ms each way and 200 Mbit/s, measured with Http2Client on a warm connection, median of 3 downloads and of 5 cancels.
  • "Buffered while paused" is what the server had sent while the body was paused. The benchmark can't measure below 1 MiB.
  • ? The loopback columns of this row are 3.1.0 itself. Its link columns use this branch with 3.1.0's 64 KiB stream window and Nagle left on.

How to read it:

  • A cancelled stream can only have let the server send its current window. With a growing window, that is about twice what the app had read at that point: 640 KiB for a response cancelled after 256 KiB, against 4 MiB before.
  • A stream that is read keeps doubling its window about once per round trip and reaches 4 MiB after about 2 MiB, so long downloads still get the large window. Fixed small windows give that up: 256 KiB caps throughput at 256 KiB per round trip.
  • The cost against a fixed 4 MiB window is the ramp-up: about 3?4 extra round trips per stream on long links. Starting at 1 MiB would ramp faster but doubles the cancel cost. 256 KiB still fits most API responses and thumbnails within the initial window, and it suits mobile links, where a big window mostly sits in the link's buffers. Changing the start is a one-constant change if reviewers prefer otherwise.

Same machine, run in ABBA order (#2031, this PR, this PR, #2031). _Reopened from #2054 after reordering performance changes behind the `3.2.1` security release._

### Summary

Fixes a performance regression against 2.3.1 / 3.1.0 introduced in 3.2.0. The incomplete field-block timeout added in #1958 creates and cancels a `Timer` for **every** inbound HEADERS and PUSH_PROMISE frame, although the whole field block has almost always arrived already. With `package:grpc` (unchanged, Dart AOT, grpc-go as the peer), upgrading http2 from 2.3.1 to #2031 (3.2.0) costs 11?21% of the throughput of small unary RPCs over h2c. Setting `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout: null` recovers all of it, and so does this PR, with the timeout still on:

| Scenario (h2c, RPC/s, median of 35 trials) | 2.3.1 | #2031 (3.2.0) | 3.2.0, `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout: null` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `unary-concurrent-16` (Dart client) | 20.6k | 16.3k (**?21%**) | 20.5k (?0%) | 20.2k (?2%) |
| `many-metadata` (Dart client) | 14.4k | 12.1k (**?16%**) | 14.3k (?1%) | 14.2k (?2%) |
| `server-unary-concurrent-128` (Dart server) | 18.6k | 16.6k (**?11%**) | 18.6k (+0%) | 18.3k (?1%) |

`FrameReader` called `onFieldBlockStart` as soon as it had parsed the 9-byte header of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame. `Connection` armed `Timer(inboundHeaderBlockTimeout)` (10 s by default) there, and cancelled it when the frame with END_HEADERS had been read, usually a few microseconds later in the same chunk of input. That is not free: in the Dart VM, adding a timer that becomes the earliest pending one, and cancelling it again, each send a message to the event handler thread to reschedule the isolate's wakeup (`_Timer._enqueue` / `_Timer.cancel` ? `_notifyEventHandler` in `sdk/lib/_internal/vm/lib/timer_impl.dart`). A busy gRPC client or server usually has no other timer pending, so every RPC paid this once (request headers, on the server) or twice (response headers and trailers, on the client). Over h2c, the Dart worker's CPU time per trial went up by 17?50% in these scenarios, and this PR brings it back to the 2.3.1 level (see below).

### Changes

- **`lib/src/frames/frame_reader.dart`**
  - The reader tracks whether it is inside a field block: from the header of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame up to the end of the frame with END_HEADERS.
  - After it has read all complete frames of a chunk of input, it calls `onFieldBlockIncomplete` (renamed from `onFieldBlockStart`; `FrameReader` is internal) if the input ended inside a field block: in the payload of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame, before a CONTINUATION frame, or inside one. A field block that starts and ends in the same chunk only gets `onFieldBlockEnd`, as before.
- **`lib/src/connection.dart`**
  - Arms the timer from `onFieldBlockIncomplete`. The rest is unchanged: the timer is not re-armed while it runs, so later chunks and CONTINUATION frames don't extend the deadline. It is cancelled when the block is complete (a cheap no-op if it was never armed), and when it fires the connection is terminated with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`.
- **`lib/transport.dart`**
  - The `Settings.inboundHeaderBlockTimeout` docs now say when the timer starts.
- **`CHANGELOG.md`**
  - Adds an entry to the `3.2.2-wip` section.

The protection stays the same. A field block that is not complete within the timeout is terminated with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`. The clock now starts when the reader runs out of input inside the block rather than when it parsed the frame header, which is at most the time it takes to parse the rest of that chunk.

### Benchmarks

`package:grpc` at 7af35c1 (the top of the open grpc-dart stack, no changes) with a `dependency_overrides` for http2. Dart 3.14.0-5.0.dev AOT, grpc-go 1.73 as the peer: Dart client vs Go server for the client scenarios, Go client vs Dart server for `server-*`. Linux Cloudtop (x64, 48 vCPU), loopback. Seven interleaved rounds with the order of the variants rotated each round, `--warmup=1 --trials=5`, so 35 trials per cell. Median (min?max); ?/? = significant (exact two-sided Mann?Whitney U, p < 0.05).

| Scenario | Proto | 2.3.1 | #2031 (3.2.0) | vs 2.3.1 | 3.2.0, timeout `null` | vs 2.3.1 | This PR | vs 2.3.1 | vs #2031 |

| `unary-concurrent-16` | h2 | 18.9k (15.1k?19.3k) | 18.3k (13.6k?19.2k) | ?3%? | 18.6k (8.8k?19.6k) | ?2% | 19.0k (14.8k?20.0k) | +1% | +3%? |
| `many-metadata` | h2c | 14.4k (11.7k?14.8k) | 12.1k (9.6k?12.5k) | ?16%? | 14.3k (10.9k?14.6k) | ?1%? | 14.2k (10.2k?14.8k) | ?2%? | **+17%?** |

  - `a-frame-split-outside-a-field-block-is-not-incomplete`: a DATA frame split across chunks after a complete HEADERS frame.
  - `headers-payload-split-across-chunks-is-incomplete`: one `incomplete` after the chunk that ends inside the HEADERS payload, then `end`.
  - `push-promise-header-without-payload-is-incomplete`: the same for a PUSH_PROMISE frame header alone.
  - `headers-waiting-for-continuation-is-incomplete`: HEADERS without END_HEADERS, then a chunk ending inside a CONTINUATION frame, then the rest. `incomplete` after each of the first two chunks, then `end`.
- `creates a field-block timer only while a field block is incomplete` (new, `test/server_test.dart`): runs a `ServerTransportConnection` in a zone that records the timers created with the configured timeout. A complete HEADERS frame creates none, and a HEADERS frame whose payload arrives later creates one, which is no longer active once the payload has arrived.

**Before fix** (new tests on the previous library code; the reader tests pass the old `onFieldBlockStart` in place of `onFieldBlockIncomplete`):
```text
00:00 +6 -1: field-block-callbacks field-blocks-within-one-chunk-are-never-incomplete [E]
  Expected: ['end', 'end']
    Actual: ['incomplete', 'end', 'incomplete', 'end']
00:00 +7 -2: field-block-callbacks a-frame-split-outside-a-field-block-is-not-incomplete [E]
  Expected: ['end']
    Actual: ['incomplete', 'end']
00:00 +9 -3: field-block-callbacks headers-waiting-for-continuation-is-incomplete [E]
  Expected: ['incomplete', 'incomplete']
    Actual: ['incomplete']
00:00 +17 -4: server-tests resource limits creates a field-block timer only while a field block is incomplete [E]
  Expected: empty
    Actual: [Instance of '_Timer']
```

(The third failure is expected: the old reader only reported the start of a field block, once.)

**After fix** (`dart test test/src/frames/frame_reader_test.dart test/server_test.dart -n 'field.block'`):
```text
00:00 +9: All tests passed!
```

> [!NOTE]
> This PR was generated by an AI coding agent (Jetski) on behalf of @mosuem.

_Reopened from #2054 after reordering performance changes behind the `3.2.1` security release._

### Summary

Fixes a performance regression against 2.3.1 / 3.1.0 introduced in 3.2.0. The incomplete field-block timeout added in #1958 creates and cancels a `Timer` for **every** inbound HEADERS and PUSH_PROMISE frame, although the whole field block has almost always arrived already. With `package:grpc` (unchanged, Dart AOT, grpc-go as the peer), upgrading http2 from 2.3.1 to #2031 (3.2.0) costs 11?21% of the throughput of small unary RPCs over h2c. Setting `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout: null` recovers all of it, and so does this PR, with the timeout still on:

| Scenario (h2c, RPC/s, median of 35 trials) | 2.3.1 | #2031 (3.2.0) | 3.2.0, `inboundHeaderBlockTimeout: null` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `unary-concurrent-16` (Dart client) | 20.6k | 16.3k (**?21%**) | 20.5k (?0%) | 20.2k (?2%) |
| `many-metadata` (Dart client) | 14.4k | 12.1k (**?16%**) | 14.3k (?1%) | 14.2k (?2%) |
| `server-unary-concurrent-128` (Dart server) | 18.6k | 16.6k (**?11%**) | 18.6k (+0%) | 18.3k (?1%) |

`FrameReader` called `onFieldBlockStart` as soon as it had parsed the 9-byte header of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame. `Connection` armed `Timer(inboundHeaderBlockTimeout)` (10 s by default) there, and cancelled it when the frame with END_HEADERS had been read, usually a few microseconds later in the same chunk of input. That is not free: in the Dart VM, adding a timer that becomes the earliest pending one, and cancelling it again, each send a message to the event handler thread to reschedule the isolate's wakeup (`_Timer._enqueue` / `_Timer.cancel` ? `_notifyEventHandler` in `sdk/lib/_internal/vm/lib/timer_impl.dart`). A busy gRPC client or server usually has no other timer pending, so every RPC paid this once (request headers, on the server) or twice (response headers and trailers, on the client). Over h2c, the Dart worker's CPU time per trial went up by 17?50% in these scenarios, and this PR brings it back to the 2.3.1 level (see below).

### Changes

- **`lib/src/frames/frame_reader.dart`**
  - The reader tracks whether it is inside a field block: from the header of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame up to the end of the frame with END_HEADERS.
  - After it has read all complete frames of a chunk of input, it calls `onFieldBlockIncomplete` (renamed from `onFieldBlockStart`; `FrameReader` is internal) if the input ended inside a field block: in the payload of a HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frame, before a CONTINUATION frame, or inside one. A field block that starts and ends in the same chunk only gets `onFieldBlockEnd`, as before.
- **`lib/src/connection.dart`**
  - Arms the timer from `onFieldBlockIncomplete`. The rest is unchanged: the timer is not re-armed while it runs, so later chunks and CONTINUATION frames don't extend the deadline. It is cancelled when the block is complete (a cheap no-op if it was never armed), and when it fires the connection is terminated with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`.
- **`lib/transport.dart`**
  - The `Settings.inboundHeaderBlockTimeout` docs now say when the timer starts.
- **`CHANGELOG.md`**
  - Adds an entry to the `3.2.2-wip` section.

The protection stays the same. A field block that is not complete within the timeout is terminated with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`. The clock now starts when the reader runs out of input inside the block rather than when it parsed the frame header, which is at most the time it takes to parse the rest of that chunk.

### Benchmarks

`package:grpc` at 7af35c1 (the top of the open grpc-dart stack, no changes) with a `dependency_overrides` for http2. Dart 3.14.0-5.0.dev AOT, grpc-go 1.73 as the peer: Dart client vs Go server for the client scenarios, Go client vs Dart server for `server-*`. Linux Cloudtop (x64, 48 vCPU), loopback. Seven interleaved rounds with the order of the variants rotated each round, `--warmup=1 --trials=5`, so 35 trials per cell. Median (min?max); ?/? = significant (exact two-sided Mann?Whitney U, p < 0.05).

| Scenario | Proto | 2.3.1 | #2031 (3.2.0) | vs 2.3.1 | 3.2.0, timeout `null` | vs 2.3.1 | This PR | vs 2.3.1 | vs #2031 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `unary-concurrent-16` | h2c | 20.6k (14.2k?21.2k) | 16.3k (14.7k?16.7k) | ?21%? | 20.5k (18.6k?21.5k) | ?0% | 20.2k (15.8k?21.1k) | ?2%? | **+24%?** |
| `unary-concurrent-16` | h2 | 18.9k (15.1k?19.3k) | 18.3k (13.6k?19.2k) | ?3%? | 18.6k (8.8k?19.6k) | ?2% | 19.0k (14.8k?20.0k) | +1% | +3%? |
| `many-metadata` | h2c | 14.4k (11.7k?14.8k) | 12.1k (9.6k?12.5k) | ?16%? | 14.3k (10.9k?14.6k) | ?1%? | 14.2k (10.2k?14.8k) | ?2%? | **+17%?** |
| `many-metadata` | h2 | 14.2k (11.5k?15.1k) | 13.1k (8.2k?14.1k) | ?7%? | 13.7k (9.5k?14.6k) | ?3%? | 13.7k (8.6k?15.2k) | ?3%? | +5%? |
| `server-unary-concurrent-128` | h2c | 18.6k (17.5k?19.2k) | 16.6k (13.8k?16.8k) | ?11%? | 18.6k (15.1k?19.0k) | +0% | 18.3k (14.7k?19.1k) | ?1% | **+11%?** |
| `server-unary-concurrent-128` | h2 | 17.9k (13.8k?18.4k) | 17.3k (13.6k?17.9k) | ?3%? | 17.5k (14.3k?18.2k) | ?2%? | 17.6k (14.7k?17.9k) | ?1%? | +2%? |

  - `field-blocks-within-one-chunk-are-never-incomplete`: HEADERS + DATA + trailers in one chunk, then HEADERS + CONTINUATION + CONTINUATION + PUSH_PROMISE in one chunk. Only `end` callbacks.
  - `a-frame-split-outside-a-field-block-is-not-incomplete`: a DATA frame split across chunks after a complete HEADERS frame.
  - `headers-payload-split-across-chunks-is-incomplete`: one `incomplete` after the chunk that ends inside the HEADERS payload, then `end`.
  - `push-promise-header-without-payload-is-incomplete`: the same for a PUSH_PROMISE frame header alone.
  - `headers-waiting-for-continuation-is-incomplete`: HEADERS without END_HEADERS, then a chunk ending inside a CONTINUATION frame, then the rest. `incomplete` after each of the first two chunks, then `end`.
- `creates a field-block timer only while a field block is incomplete` (new, `test/server_test.dart`): runs a `ServerTransportConnection` in a zone that records the timers created with the configured timeout. A complete HEADERS frame creates none, and a HEADERS frame whose payload arrives later creates one, which is no longer active once the payload has arrived.

**Before fix** (new tests on the previous library code; the reader tests pass the old `onFieldBlockStart` in place of `onFieldBlockIncomplete`):
```text
00:00 +6 -1: field-block-callbacks field-blocks-within-one-chunk-are-never-incomplete [E]
  Expected: ['end', 'end']
    Actual: ['incomplete', 'end', 'incomplete', 'end']
00:00 +7 -2: field-block-callbacks a-frame-split-outside-a-field-block-is-not-incomplete [E]
  Expected: ['end']
    Actual: ['incomplete', 'end']
00:00 +9 -3: field-block-callbacks headers-waiting-for-continuation-is-incomplete [E]
  Expected: ['incomplete', 'incomplete']
    Actual: ['incomplete']
00:00 +17 -4: server-tests resource limits creates a field-block timer only while a field block is incomplete [E]
  Expected: empty

```

timeline.message:
fix(http2): Http2Client disables Nagle's algorithm and grows each stream's receive window from 256 KiB

Fixes two Http2Client performance regressions against 3.1.0, found with
package:http_client_benchmarks and bisected to their commits:

- download-cancel (cancel a response after 256 KiB, then make one more
  request on the same client): ~1 ms in 3.1.0, ~26 ms since #2029. With a
  fixed 4 MiB stream window the server has already sent up to 4 MiB of the
  cancelled response, all of which must be read off the shared connection
  before the next response. Each stream's receive window now starts at
  256 KiB and doubles every time half of it has been read, up to 4 MiB: a
  response that is cancelled (or paused) early has only let the server send a
  little, while a long download still reaches the 4 MiB window.
- upload-1mib-sequential: 27.7 MB/s in 3.1.0, 20.7 MB/s since #1999.
  Http2Client never disabled Nagle's algorithm, which holds back the short
  tail of a write until the earlier data is acknowledged, while the server
  delays that acknowledgement (by 40 ms on Linux) waiting for the rest of the
  frame. Since #1999 an upload is sent as one large DATA frame, so this
  stalled nearly every upload. Http2Client now sets TCP_NODELAY, as dart:io's
  HttpClient and HttpServer do; that also removes the same stall from many
  other requests (e.g. head-of-line latency 24 ms -> 2.6 ms on Linux).

The growing window is internal to Http2Client: ClientConnection (not
exported) takes a maxStreamWindowSize that the stream handler passes to each
stream's IncomingWindowHandler.
